diff --git a/crates/callisto-model/src/ecosystem.rs b/crates/callisto-model/src/ecosystem.rs
index 4c58043c..c1b4d2de 100644
--- a/crates/callisto-model/src/ecosystem.rs
+++ b/crates/callisto-model/src/ecosystem.rs
@@ -134,7 +134,10 @@ impl PublishTarget {
     /// The `publish-to` config string this variant parses from, mirroring
     /// `parse_publish_target` in `callisto_graph::config::resolve`. Used to
     /// name the mismatched target in diagnostics/errors without leaking the
-    /// `Debug` representation of the variant's payload.
+    /// `Debug` representation of the variant's payload, and doubles as the
+    /// semantic-fingerprint "kind" string (`target_fingerprint` in
+    /// `callisto_graph::commands::release`) since both need the exact same
+    /// stable, variant-identifying string.
     pub fn config_str(&self) -> &'static str {
         match self {
             PublishTarget::CratesIo => "crates-io",
@@ -145,6 +148,38 @@ impl PublishTarget {
             PublishTarget::None => "none",
         }
     }
+
+    /// The operator's explicit registry/index/source override carried by
+    /// this variant's payload, if any -- `Npm.registry`, `Pypi.index`, and
+    /// `NuGet.source` are all "the same field" for this purpose. `CratesIo`,
+    /// `GitHubRelease`, and `None` carry no such override.
+    pub fn registry_override(&self) -> Option<&str> {
+        match self {
+            PublishTarget::Npm { registry, .. } => registry.as_deref(),
+            PublishTarget::Pypi { index } => index.as_deref(),
+            PublishTarget::NuGet { source } => source.as_deref(),
+            PublishTarget::CratesIo | PublishTarget::GitHubRelease | PublishTarget::None => None,
+        }
+    }
+
+    /// Whether this target has a real dispatch implementation today.
+    ///
+    /// `PublishTarget` and `Ecosystem` are not 1:1: `GitHubRelease` is a VCS
+    /// release action with no backing package `Ecosystem` at all, and `None`
+    /// is the "not configured to publish" sentinel, not a real target --
+    /// neither can defer to `Ecosystem::is_implemented()`. Every other
+    /// variant carries a package ecosystem ([`Self::ecosystem`]) and defers
+    /// to that ecosystem's own implementedness.
+    pub fn is_implemented(&self) -> bool {
+        match self {
+            PublishTarget::None => true,
+            PublishTarget::GitHubRelease => false,
+            PublishTarget::CratesIo
+            | PublishTarget::Npm { .. }
+            | PublishTarget::Pypi { .. }
+            | PublishTarget::NuGet { .. } => self.ecosystem().is_some_and(|ecosystem| ecosystem.is_implemented()),
+        }
+    }
 }
 
 /// PEP 503 / PEP 427 style Python package-name normalization: lowercase,
@@ -231,4 +266,57 @@ mod tests {
         assert_eq!(normalize_pypi_package_name("foo-.-bar"), "foo_bar");
         assert_eq!(normalize_pypi_package_name("foo___bar"), "foo_bar");
     }
+
+    #[test]
+    fn publish_target_registry_override_extracts_payload_field() {
+        assert_eq!(PublishTarget::CratesIo.registry_override(), None);
+        assert_eq!(
+            PublishTarget::Npm {
+                registry: Some("https://npm.example.com".to_string()),
+                access: None
+            }
+            .registry_override(),
+            Some("https://npm.example.com")
+        );
+        assert_eq!(
+            PublishTarget::Npm {
+                registry: None,
+                access: None
+            }
+            .registry_override(),
+            None
+        );
+        assert_eq!(
+            PublishTarget::Pypi {
+                index: Some("https://pypi.example.com".to_string())
+            }
+            .registry_override(),
+            Some("https://pypi.example.com")
+        );
+        assert_eq!(
+            PublishTarget::NuGet {
+                source: Some("https://nuget.example.com".to_string())
+            }
+            .registry_override(),
+            Some("https://nuget.example.com")
+        );
+        assert_eq!(PublishTarget::GitHubRelease.registry_override(), None);
+        assert_eq!(PublishTarget::None.registry_override(), None);
+    }
+
+    #[test]
+    fn publish_target_is_implemented_matches_dispatchable_variants() {
+        assert!(PublishTarget::CratesIo.is_implemented());
+        assert!(PublishTarget::Npm {
+            registry: None,
+            access: None
+        }
+        .is_implemented());
+        assert!(PublishTarget::Pypi { index: None }.is_implemented());
+        assert!(!PublishTarget::NuGet { source: None }.is_implemented());
+        assert!(!PublishTarget::GitHubRelease.is_implemented());
+        // `None` is vacuously "implemented" -- there is nothing to dispatch,
+        // so it must never trip a `PublishTargetNotImplemented` diagnostic.
+        assert!(PublishTarget::None.is_implemented());
+    }
 }

1. `WorkspaceCargoResolver::write_version`/`write_dependency` no longer call `persist` internally — pure in-memory mutation now, matching `CargoToml`/`PackageJson`/`PyprojectToml`. `persist` is promoted to `pub`. **Hazard investigation (required reading, done first):** Read `WorkspaceCargoResolver` (`crates/callisto-manifests/src/cargo.rs`), `classify_manifest_writes`/`apply_version_plan` (`crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs`), `cascade.rs`'s `CargoWorkspaceDependency` emission, and `.claude/plans/ACTIVE.md`'s "Track: apply_version_plan write-batching" entry plus `crates/callisto-graph/tests/apply_batch_002_verification_notes.md`. The original exclusion's hazard is specifically the **mixed-routing** case — a root `Cargo.toml` written through *both* the `Manifest` trait (e.g. a self-referential root package's own `[package]`/`[dependencies]`) *and* `WorkspaceCargoResolver` (`[workspace.package]`/`[workspace.dependencies]`) in the *same plan*. That is a different case from the one I batched (pure-resolver-only paths, no competing `Manifest`-trait write in the plan). I left the mixed-routing exclusion (`classification.excluded`) completely untouched — it still forces fully individual, unbatched, plan-order processing on both sides — and added a regression test (`mixed_routing_root_manifest_still_persists_resolver_writes_individually`) proving it still isn't batched.

**Fix:**
1. `WorkspaceCargoResolver::write_version`/`write_dependency` no longer call `persist` internally — pure in-memory mutation now, matching `CargoToml`/`PackageJson`/`PyprojectToml`. `persist` is promoted to `pub`. Updated the one other call site that relied on the implicit persist (`CargoToml::update_dependency_spec`'s inherited-dependency delegation) to call `.persist(permit)` explicitly. Full-workspace grep confirmed no other call sites exist anywhere in the repo.
2. `classify_manifest_writes`/`apply_version_plan` (`crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs`) gained a `resolver_batched` group: a root manifest written only via `CargoWorkspacePackage`/`CargoWorkspaceDependency` (no mixed routing) is now opened once, mutated in memory for its bump + all rewrites, and persisted exactly once.

**Permit accounting:** `ApplyPermit` is a zero-sized `Copy` capability token threaded by shared reference — there's no separate permit ledger in this codebase, so "permit accounting" resolves to counting `atomic_write`/`persist` invocations. Added `resolver_load_call_count`/`resolver_persist_call_count` counters, kept deliberately separate from the existing `open_call_count`/`persist_call_count` (which are scoped to the `Manifest` trait's three implementors) because `OpenContext::for_workspace_root` calls `WorkspaceCargoResolver::load` unconditionally on every `apply_version_plan` call whenever the workspace root has a `Cargo.toml` — folding the counters together would have broken essentially every existing `open_call_count` assertion in the crate (verified this empirically before choosing separate counters).

**Before/after evidence** (`crates/callisto-graph/tests/apply_persist_open_count_test.rs`, new test `resolver_batched_root_manifest_opens_once_and_persists_once_for_bump_plus_multiple_rewrites`): a plan with 1 workspace-version bump + 3 inherited-dependency rewrites sharing one root manifest now produces `resolver_load_call_count() == 2` (1 incidental `for_workspace_root` load + 1 batched-loop load) and `resolver_persist_call_count() == 1` — down from what would have been 5 loads / 4 persists before this fix (1 incidental + one load+persist per write).

**Verification:** `cargo test -p callisto-manifests -p callisto-graph` — all green (569 tests across both crates' unit + integration suites, including all pre-existing `WorkspaceCargoResolver`/`apply_version_plan`/cascade-pipeline tests, unchanged in outcome). `cargo clippy -p callisto-manifests -p callisto-graph --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean. Also ran full-workspace `cargo build`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check`, and `callisto-cli`'s `lifecycle_e2e_tests`/`durable_release_e2e_tests` — all clean, as extra confirmation beyond the two required crates.

**Changeset:** `.changeset/workspace-cargo-resolver-batch-writes.md` (patch, `callisto-manifests` + `callisto-graph`), validated via `cargo run -p callisto-cli -- validate`.</result>

cd /tmp/callisto-pr6 && gh pr create --title "refactor(format,manifests,graph,model): bump-arithmetic unification, resolver write batching, PublishTarget capability unification" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary

Three findings from the second-round audit, batched into one PR — different crates, no file overlap, each independently verified before combining.

- **`callisto-format/bump.rs`**: `SemVerVersioning::bump`/`Pep440Versioning::bump` implemented the identical zero-guard major.minor.patch arithmetic, one on `Version`, one on a raw `(u64,u64,u64)` triple; `bump_prerelease` duplicated the same "finalize, scan for trailing counter, increment, reassemble" pattern again. Git history shows two independent bug-fix commits were needed for the same arithmetic on each copy. Extracted `bump_release_triple` and `next_counter`, used by both grammars. Pure refactor — traced the `Severity::None` early-return path in both callers by hand to confirm the shared helper's `unreachable!()` is genuinely unreachable, not a latent panic.
- **`callisto-manifests`/`callisto-graph`**: `WorkspaceCargoResolver::write_version`/`write_dependency` each called `persist()` internally, unlike every other `Manifest` impl — so `apply_version_plan` had to process each workspace-root Cargo.toml write individually, causing N+1 read/parse/write cycles on the same file for a release touching the workspace version plus several inherited-dependency rewrites. Split into pure in-memory mutation + explicit `persist()`, matching the existing pattern. **This is the highest-risk change in the PR** (permit accounting, atomic-write guarantees) — the existing mixed-routing data-loss hazard exclusion (a root manifest written through both the `Manifest` trait and `WorkspaceCargoResolver` in the same plan) is deliberately left untouched and has its own regression test proving it still isn't batched; only the pure-resolver-only case is now batched. New call-count counters prove the shared root manifest is opened once and persisted once regardless of how many bumps/rewrites target it.
- **`callisto-model`/`callisto-graph`**: `PublishTarget` capability (fingerprint kind, registry override, dispatchability) was encoded independently in three match statements. Extended the existing `ecosystem.rs` capability layer instead of inventing a second one — confirmed `PublishTarget`↔`Ecosystem` isn't 1:1 (`GitHubRelease` has no backing ecosystem, `None` is a sentinel) and designed `is_implemented()`/`registry_override()` around that explicitly, with tests covering both special cases.

## Test plan

- [x] Each fix independently verified (own tests, own scoped `cargo test`/`clippy --all-targets`) before combining — the resolver-batching fix in particular got an extra independent full-suite verification pass given its risk profile
- [x] `cargo nextest run --workspace --all-features`: 1291/1291 passed
- [x] `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean
- [x] `just fmt-check`: clean
- [x] 3 changesets added (patch-level: `callisto-format`; `callisto-manifests`+`callisto-graph`; `callisto-model`+`callisto-graph`)

input.name: fix-f20-batch-git-cat-file
input.description: Batch git show calls into cat-file --batch
input.prompt:
Callisto is a Rust monorepo release/versioning engine. You're fixing one confirmed performance finding from an audit, in an isolated git worktree branched from `main` (check `git log -3` to confirm your base — recent PRs through #72 should be present).

**Finding**: `crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_decision.rs`, function `derive_release_commit_decision`. Since only two distinct commits are ever queried (`parent` and `release_commit`), all of those blob reads could be satisfied by two `git cat-file --batch` invocations (one per commit, streaming every needed path's blob in one process) instead of 2N separate `git show` invocations.

**Fix**: replace the per-manifest `manifest_version_at(parent)` / `manifest_version_at(release_commit)` pair with a batched approach: collect every canonical manifest path needed for BOTH commits up front, then issue exactly two `git cat-file --batch` invocations (one per commit) that stream back every requested path's blob content (or "missing" for a path that doesn't exist in that commit — a package's manifest may not have existed at `parent` if it was newly added), and parse the version out of each result the same way `manifest_version_at` currently does. Check how `CommandRunner`/`git_stdout` feeds subprocess stdin/stdout in this file and elsewhere in `callisto-vcs`/`callisto-graph` for the established pattern of piping input to a subprocess and reading its output (search for any existing `--batch`/stdin-piping usage in the workspace as a model, or design a clean one if none exists).

1. Read `release_decision.rs`'s full `derive_release_commit_decision` function and `manifest_version_at` before changing anything. Understand exactly what `git cat-file --batch`'s input/output protocol looks like (`<object>\n` lines on stdin, `<sha> <type> <size>\n<content>\n` or `<object> missing\n` on stdout) so your parsing is correct, including the case where a manifest path doesn't exist at one of the two commits.
2. This function is part of the release-decision trust boundary (verifies a release commit's claimed version roster against the actual diff) — a subtle parsing bug here would be a real security/correctness regression, not just a perf issue. 3. All existing tests for `derive_release_commit_decision` (including its `FixedBlobRunner` test double, if that's how tests inject git responses — check for it) must pass unchanged in outcome, or be updated to reflect the new subprocess call shape if they assert on the exact command invoked. If tests inject responses via a mock `CommandRunner`, update the mock's expected invocations to match the new `cat-file --batch` calls instead of per-manifest `git show` calls.

5. Run `cargo test -p callisto-graph` and `cargo clippy -p callisto-graph --all-targets -- -D warnings`. Both must be clean.

input.description: Decide and apply test-counter gating policy
input.prompt:
Callisto is a Rust monorepo release/versioning engine. You're investigating and (if appropriate) fixing one architecture finding from an audit, in an isolated git worktree branched from `main` (check `git log -3` to confirm your base — recent PRs through #72 should be present).

They are NOT gated behind `#[cfg(test)]` or a `test-util` Cargo feature — they're plain `pub` items in the crate's real, shipped API surface, and the counter increments unconditionally inside the real per-commit revwalk loop (a production hot path). The original audit flagged this as a policy gap and specifically noted a prior precedent already existed for this same pattern: `callisto_manifests::open_call_count`.

**This needs fresh investigation, not a reflexive fix — the situation has likely changed.** Since that finding was written, this same "process-global test-observability counter, `pub`, ungated, incremented in real production code, with a `reset_*`/`*_count` accessor pair" pattern has been deliberately added several MORE times across the workspace as an accepted, precedented convention — search the workspace for other examples (you should find at least: `callisto_manifests::open_call_count`/`reset_open_call_count`, `callisto_manifests::persist_call_count`, `callisto_manifests::resolver_load_call_count`/`resolver_persist_call_count`, `callisto_graph::identity::identity_read_count`/`reset_identity_read_count`, and possibly others — find them all). | `callisto-manifests` | `PERSIST_CALL_COUNT` / `persist_call_count()` / `reset_persist_call_count()` | `src/lib.rs:198-208` | same crate |

| `callisto-graph` | `GLOB_COMPILE_COUNT` / `glob_compile_count()` / `reset_glob_compile_count()` | `src/tags.rs:58-74` | same crate |
| `callisto-vcs` | `REVWALK_VISIT_COUNT` / `revwalk_visit_count()` / `reset_revwalk_visit_count()` | `src/lib.rs:222-232` (the finding in question) | Yes (0.5.0, MIT OR Apache-2.0) |

`callisto_manifests::open_call_count` is explicitly the *named precedent* — every later instance's doc comment cross-references it by name ("Mirrors `callisto_manifests::open_call_count`", "Process-global, like `callisto_manifests::reset_open_call_count`", "same precedent as `callisto_manifests::open_call_count`"). This is not incidental convergence; it's a deliberately copied, self-documenting pattern.

**On the "external reachability" hypothesis (checked and refuted):** I verified via crates.io's API that `callisto-vcs`, `callisto-manifests`, and `callisto-graph` are **all** actually published, multi-version, independently-installable crates (`callisto-vcs` 0.3.1→0.5.0, `callisto-manifests` 0.3.0→0.5.0, `callisto-graph` 0.3.1→0.5.0 — all on crates.io right now with real download counts). So there is no reachability asymmetry — every instance is equally exposed to the same class of external consumer. If anything, `callisto-manifests` (AGPL-3.0-only) carries a *stronger* copyleft obligation on anyone who depends on it than `callisto-vcs` (permissive MIT/Apache-2.0), so the "risk profile" argument actually cuts the opposite direction from what the original finding implied.

This is a consistent, deliberate choice across the whole family, not an inconsistency isolated to `callisto-vcs`.

(a) The help text lies about an already-published package. release.rs:355-368: npm publish succeeds, then `npm_version_is_published` runs `npm view`. If that read-back fails for any reason other than a recognized 404/ETARGET string — registry 503, `ENEEDAUTH`, network timeout — line 409 returns `ReleaseIntentStale`. The operator sees:

Both sentences are false: the workspace snapshot is unchanged, and the package is live on npm. The operation remains Attempting for reconciliation rather than asserting a release the registry cannot yet prove exists." (b) A gpg misconfiguration is reported as tamper detection. release.rs:439: `git.create_tag(...).map_err(|_error| GraphError::ReleaseIntentStale)?`. ## Why this specifically defeats the persist-and-verify redesign's purpose
The redesign exists to separate a legitimately stale or tampered intent from everything else. As written, an operator cannot distinguish: a genuine tamper/staleness rejection; a parse bug in `manifest_version_at` on an unusual manifest shape; a transient registry outage after a successful publish; or a local gpg/credential misconfiguration. All four print an identical two-line message under an identical E124 code with identical remediation advice — correct for exactly one of them, actively harmful for the other three.

## Suggested shape (not implemented — read-only pass)
Give the variant a source, matching the neighboring E136 pattern, and split execution-time failures into a distinct variant whose help text does not claim "no release operation was authorized" (e.g. `ReleaseDispatchFailed { operation: ReleaseOperationId, #[source] source }`). Scenario (a) warrants its own variant — "published but not yet confirmable by the registry" is a third state the current type cannot represent at all.

A huge wave landed — 45+ verdicts now in. The headline: **the overwhelming majority were correctly refuted with rigorous evidence** (traced control flow, cited exact guard lines, in several cases empirically tested against the pinned crate version). That's a good signal — it means the codebase is more solid than the raw scanner output suggested. Still waiting on a few stragglers (F20, `ADV-PANIC-002`, a handful of unwrap verdicts, boundary-tracer's full output) before final synthesis, but here's what's real so far:

**Confirmed, worth fixing:**
1. **`ReleaseOperationId`'s `Ord` still has the class of bug PR #64/F5 was supposed to eliminate** — its own fix left `self.version.render()` (raw string) in the comparison tuple instead of comparing `Version` properly, so two operations with the same rendered string under different grammars (SemVer vs PEP 440) still collide as a false `DuplicateOperation`. Surfaced as an adjacent finding while refuting `ADV-PANIC-006`.
2. **pnpm/npm workspace glob negation (`!pattern`) silently mishandled** — empirically verified against the pinned `globset` version. `packages: ['packages/**', '!**/test/**']` (a real pnpm doc example) admits *everything*, including the excluded test packages, with zero diagnostic. Can cause an explicitly-excluded package to get versioned/released.
3. **`ConfigProvenance` tracking is entirely dead code** — recorded for 5 config keys, but its only consumer (`attribution_line`) has zero callers anywhere. This is a spec-mandated feature (docs/00-design.md §13 invariant 28) that was built end-to-end and never wired into any renderer.
4. **`GraphError::ReleaseIntentStale`'s catch-all is confirmed architecturally harmful**, not just untidy — its own help text ("no release operation was authorized") is provably false at ~15 dispatch-time sites that run *after* an intent was already validated and accepted, including a scenario where an npm publish succeeds and a transient registry read-back failure gets reported as "regenerate your stale intent."
5. **`add.rs`'s severity-error message is factually wrong** — says "must be patch, minor, or major" but `none` (any casing) is silently accepted too.
6. A **possible 4th missed sibling** in `cascade.rs`'s `raise()` function — a fixed-sibling loop that may lack the same stale-member guard PR #64 added elsewhere in the same file. Needs verification against the actual diff before I trust it.

Want me to keep collecting the stragglers and then batch the real, well-scoped ones (1, 5, and verifying 6) into another PR, while flagging 2, 3, and 4 as bigger design conversations rather than quick fixes?

Another real bug surfaced as a byproduct: **`cascade.rs:414` passes the unfiltered group `g` into `fixed_group_target`, not the `live_members` list the surrounding block already computed.** So a stale member that still has a leftover git tag can become `released[0]` and silently drive the whole group's alignment base to a wrong `1.0.0` substitution — a real wrong-version bug distinct from the panic PR #64 already fixed, since it's silent-fallback/ordering rather than a crash.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The overarching thread across this entire session has been a second-round adversarial audit of the Callisto Rust monorepo (a release/versioning engine), triggered by the user's request: *"Shall we do another round of analysis to look for things we may have missed? Bugs lurking in the codebase, duplicated code, identical code paths that should be united? Performance issues, architectural gaps?"* This produced two parallel audit tracks (a `ranger:audit` bug-hunt pipeline and a custom duplication/performance/architecture Workflow yielding 29 verified findings), which the user then directed me to fix in batched, parallelized PRs, explicitly requesting file-overlap-aware grouping ("Can it be one PR?"). Mid-session, the user escalated to a meta-level complaint about recurring mistakes (*"Weeks now just bug hunting our own bugs, adding more to the pile as we fix things partially and leave just as much of a mess behind"*) and *"How do we fix this systemically, not just this repo though?... it's still making stupid mistakes, specially in claude but I'm sure in codex too"* — driving process fixes to CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, the `.agents/` bug-hunter agents, and the actual `orin-dx/agent-plugins` source repo (both Claude-native and Codex-native definitions), explicitly correcting me once: *"We don't want to modify the copied/installed version here."* The user also stated a durable process rule: *"We should not leave things as draft after implemented BTW."* Most recently, the user requested: *"Can we tackle the P3 items in a single PR now and look at the shortlist in a parallel agent team keeping in mind to use the best model and effort for the tasks?"* — driving the current in-flight work of 4 P3 fix agents plus a 52-candidate + 1 boundary-tracer ranger:adversary sweep of the earlier-triaged shortlist.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Ranger audit pipeline (recon→scanner→boundary-tracer[conditional]→adversary→exit-gate), with `ranger:adversary`'s hard rule "Invoke once per candidate... Never batch," and each ranger subagent type carrying its own baked-in model/effort tier (recon: haiku/low, scanner/boundary-tracer: sonnet/medium, adversary/exit-gate: opus/high) — respected by omitting a `model` override when dispatching these specific subagent_types.
   - Candidate@1 / finding-report@1 schemas; "field survival map" as boundary-tracer's specific output for T7 (Write-Only Fields) and T10 (Error Downgrade) candidates.
   - Git worktree isolation (`isolation: "worktree"` on Agent calls) for parallel fix-agent dispatch; read-only investigation agents (ranger:adversary/boundary-tracer) need no isolation since they never edit files and can share the main `main` checkout concurrently.
   - Established verification discipline (self-imposed, applied consistently): never trust an agent's prose summary — always `git show <sha>` the actual diff myself, then independently rerun `cargo test`/`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` before cherry-picking into a consolidated branch, then rerun the full workspace suite on the consolidated branch before push/PR.
   - Cherry-pick consolidation pattern: create a fresh worktree off `origin/main`, cherry-pick each verified fix-agent's commit SHA in sequence, run full CI, push, `gh pr create`, then `git worktree remove --force` cleanup for every worktree used (fix-agent worktrees + consolidation worktree).
   - RTK global hook (rewrites bare `git` to `rtk git`) breaking inside worktree-isolated subagents — workaround: use `/usr/bin/git` (or `/opt/homebrew/bin/git`) explicitly; if an agent hits a *different* permission-classifier denial (not the worktree-isolation one) after attempting a workaround (e.g., editing rtk config), it must NOT retry alternate forms or touch config — must stop, leave edits uncommitted, and let the coordinator (me) commit from my own session context instead.

# Callisto Codebase Guide for Claude & AI Agents

This repository follows the centralized AI agent guidelines documented in [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md).

---

## Quick Reference

### Primary Task Runner Commands
- `just` / `just ci-fast` (default): Full verification suite minus `coverage`. Use this for everyday pre-PR checks.
- `just ci`: Same, plus `coverage`. Matches CI parity; slow (coverage recompiles the whole workspace under instrumentation).
- `just test` / `moon run :test`: Run all unit, integration, doctests, and E2E lifecycle test suites.
- `just lint` / `moon run :lint`: Run Clippy lints with `-D warnings`.
- `just fmt` / `moon run :format`: Format code automatically.

### Key Architectural Invariants
1. **Safe Rust Only**: `unsafe_code = "forbid"` across all crates.
2. **Format Preservation**: Manifest modifications use CST editors (`toml_edit`, `serde_json` indentation fingerprinting).
3. **Atomic File Persistence**: File edits use `callisto_model::atomic::atomic_write`.
4. **Layer Isolation**: Layer 1 crates (`callisto-model`, `callisto-format`) must remain permissive (`MIT OR Apache-2.0`) and never depend on AGPL crates.
5. **No Emojis in Documentation**: Keep docs clean, technical, scannable, and emoji-free.

### Build/test scoping
Full pipeline: `just ci`/`just test`/`just lint`. For scoped iteration, one direct `cargo test -p <crate>` / `cargo clippy -p <crate>` invocation -- not `moon run <project>:test`, whose per-project fan-out serializes on `target/`'s build lock (see `Justfile`'s `lint` comment; `moon`'s own `test`/`lint` tasks are literally `cargo test -p $project` / `cargo clippy -p $project` each).

### `Cargo.lock`
Never `git checkout -- Cargo.lock` as pre-commit cleanup -- thrashes the build cache, can turn `just ci` into a multi-hour run. A diff means investigate, not discard.

name: implement
description: Execute an approved plan or specification with targeted implementation, tests, evidence, review, and independent verification. Use for “implement this”, “execute the plan”, “build this feature”, “write the code”, or “refactor without changing behavior”.
---

# Implement with evidence

## Outcome

Make the requested workspace change in bounded batches and return a scoped verdict grounded in current code, risk-based verification, and defect-family review.

## Workflow

1. Prefer a persisted `plan@1`. Read it from `plan_file_path` and its source spec from `spec_file_path`; validate them with `shared/schemas/plan@1.json` and `shared/schemas/spec@1.json`.
2. Verify the plan’s `spec_hash` against the raw spec file bytes. Stop and report drift if it differs; a stale plan cannot silently govern implementation.
3. Produce `workspace-manifest@1` from current repository state, every affected language, project-native verification capabilities, baseline tests, and exposed workflow provenance.
4. Execute one cohesive subsystem batch. Choose the smallest safe implementation and verification methods from the changed risks and `shared/references/verification-evidence.md`.
5. Record `implementation-result@1` with exact criterion locations, commands, observations, boundaries, and environment evidence.
6. Use available mutation tooling against changed behavior or a safe deliberate-fault check. Record `mutation-report@2`; unavailable evidence is a coverage gap.
7. Produce `implementation-review@2`. Judge verification fit, sibling completeness, semantic models, and architecture.
8. Before completion, account for every planned batch and started verification task, reread persisted artifacts and current code, independently challenge semantic completeness, and emit scoped `verdict@3`. Commit only after user authorization.

## Defect-family review

Before reviewing, load `shared/references/implementation-review.md` and the evidence it selects. For each changed defect, assess:

- Syntactic siblings with the same code shape or algorithm.
- Semantic siblings with the same domain responsibility or failure state.
- Candidate sites supporting semantic completeness, including zero-match claims.
- The shared root cause for related instances.
- Missing concepts, states, operations, boundaries, abstractions, invariants, or enforcement.
- One disposition: fix instances, unify implementation, escalate architecture, or explicitly defer.
- Boundary reach, input-space method, relevant environments, external-state freshness, and coverage gaps.

Use the current architecture model when available to derive candidate responsibilities and canonical abstractions. Resolve `changes_requested` findings before the exit gate. Route `needs_architecture` to `scribe:architect`; gate the resulting spec, amend the plan, then resume.

## Contract

- Input schemas: `shared/schemas/plan@1.json` and `shared/schemas/spec@1.json`
- Workspace schema: `shared/schemas/workspace-manifest@1.json`
- Batch schema: `shared/schemas/implementation-result@1.json`
- Mutation schema: `shared/schemas/mutation-report@2.json`
- Review schema: `shared/schemas/implementation-review@2.json`
- Output schema: `shared/schemas/verdict@3.json`
- Durable inputs: `docs/projects/<linked_spec>.json` and `docs/specs/<id>.json` when their path fields are set
- Evidence: per-task `criteria_evidence` points to current implementation and tests; it is not a substitute for final inspection.

## Teams and fallback

Before delegating, read `agent-roles/README.md`; use `implementer` only for an isolated batch and `reviewer` only after its diff and verification output exist.

Use teams only for independent subsystem batches with no shared files or undecided interfaces. Give each teammate a batch, criteria, current manifest, and persisted paths. Reconcile changed files and observed outputs; track every started task to a terminal result. Work alone for coupled boundaries or when teams are unavailable.

## Exceptions and recovery

- If the implementation contradicts a spec criterion, halt remaining work and report `spec_contradiction` with the criterion ID, spec claim, observed behavior, and evidence. Route the correction to `scribe:correct-spec`, then replan in amend mode.
- If the safe solution needs an architectural boundary beyond plan scope, stop that batch and report an architecture escalation grounded in live code. Do not commit an unsafe shape just to complete the plan.
- If related defects reveal a missing domain concept, state, operation, boundary, abstraction, invariant, or enforcement mechanism, route `implementation-review@2` to `scribe:architect` before continuing.
- If one batch cannot be implemented safely within plan scope, route its `implementation-result@1` architecture escalation to `scribe:architect`.
- If a test or build fails, diagnose from the observed output and fix only the relevant defect before continuing. Do not mask a failure by weakening verification.

## Boundaries

- Do not make external releases, push branches, or commit without user authorization.
- Do not claim success from a passing targeted test when the applicable full suite has not been considered.
- Do not accept teammate summaries without reading the changed files, test output, and evidence yourself.
- Do not require mutation, property, fuzz, boundary, or environment checks when the changed risk does not justify them.
- Do not claim support from a named tool alone; record what it exercised and observed.

cd /Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/p3-consolidation
gh pr create --title "perf(graph),refactor(model): P3 batch — git-cat-file batching, schema-gate dedup, newtype macro dedup" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary

Three independently-verified P3 findings from the second-round audit, bundled into one PR per the file-overlap-aware grouping convention used for prior audit batches.

- **F20** — `derive_release_commit_decision` replaces its old 2N-`git-show`-calls loop with two `git cat-file --batch` calls (`batch_manifest_blobs_at`/`resolve_batch_versions`/`parse_manifest_version` in `callisto-graph/src/commands/release_decision.rs`). Adds `CommandRunner::run_with_stdin` (backward-compatible default impl) and `CliCommandRunner::run_with_stdin` with a dedicated writer thread to avoid pipe deadlock on large payloads. The batch parser fails closed on every framing ambiguity (malformed header, non-hex sha, wrong object type, size overflow, missing separator, trailing output) and is UTF-8-boundary-safe.
- **F27** — new `callisto_model::release::check_schema_version` helper dedups the schema-version gate that was hand-rolled across 6 `Deserialize` impls (`ReleaseDecisionV1`, `ReleaseIntentV1`, `ReleasePrConfigV1`, `ReleasePrSnapshotV2`, `ReleasePrDecisionV2`, `ReleasePrCommitPlanV1`).
- **F28** — new `string_newtype!`/`string_newtype_display!` macros in `callisto-model/src/identity.rs` dedup `GroupName`/`RegistryKey` boilerplate. `TagName` (in `tag.rs`) keeps its custom validating `Serialize`/`Deserialize` and `parse`/`new_unchecked` untouched (it validates on deserialize, unlike the other two) — only its `as_str`/`Display` pair adopts the shared macro.

## Test plan
- [x] `cargo nextest run --workspace --all-features` — 1295 passed, 0 skipped
- [x] `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- [x] `just fmt-check` — clean
- [x] Each fix independently reviewed against its source diff (not agent summaries) before cherry-pick

https://claude.ai/code/REDACTED
EOF
)" 2>&1

**Taxonomy claim:** Silent Unwrap Fallbacks — major/minor/patch default to 0 after only a grammar check, not a component-presence check, gating the actual bump computation.

## Refutation

The candidate assumes the grammar tag and the parsed payload inside `Version` are independent, so that a `SemVer`-tagged version could hold a payload with a missing component. They are inseparable by construction. For SemVer, the grammar check **is** a component-presence proof.

**1. Grammar is pinned before line 66.** `bump.rs:55-60` returns `BumpError::NotSemVer` unless `current.grammar() == VersionGrammar::SemVer`. At line 66 the tag is necessarily `SemVer`.

**2. The tag and payload cannot diverge.** `Version` (`/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/version.rs:29-34`) has all-`pub(crate)` fields, so only `callisto-model` can construct one. `ParsedVersion` is constructed in exactly three places, all in `version.rs`, each pairing tag with matching payload:

- `parse`, SemVer arm (`version.rs:45-49`): `grammar: SemVer` + `ParsedVersion::SemVer`
- `parse`, Pep440 arm (`version.rs:66-70`): `grammar: Pep440` + `ParsedVersion::Pep440`
- `Version::semver` (`version.rs:82-86`): `grammar: SemVer` + `ParsedVersion::SemVer`

`Deserialize` (`version.rs:178-186`) routes through `parse`. A repo-wide grep for `ParsedVersion::` outside `version.rs` returns zero hits — no other crate, and no other function in this crate, can build the mismatched combination.

**3. The accessors are unconditional on that variant.** `version.rs:103`, `:110`, `:117` are `Some(v.major)` / `Some(v.minor)` / `Some(v.patch)`, reading `semver::Version`'s plain `u64` fields. Only the `Pep440` arm can return `None`, via `release().get(n)` on a short release vector.

**Conclusion:** no input can reach line 66 with a missing component. `semver::Version::parse("1.2")` fails outright at step 2, and there is no other entry point. The `unwrap_or(0)` is unreachable-default code; no unintended bumped version can be computed through it. No concrete failing scenario exists to state.

Per the workspace guidance on structurally identical code, I checked the PEP 440 analogue where `None` genuinely can occur: `release_triple` at `bump.rs:289-296`. PEP 440 permits a short release segment (`"1.2"`, `"1"`), so its `unwrap_or(0)` is reachable. That defaulting is documented, intended policy rather than a silent wrong answer — the module doc at `bump.rs:24-25` states the release segment is normalized to `major.minor.patch`. `1.2` + Patch → `1.2.1`; `1` + Minor → `1.1.0`. Every result is strictly greater than its input and matches operator intent. Not a defect either; no follow-up needed.

## Bug 1: Poetry-style PEP 508 specs silently dropped from the dependency graph

File: `crates/callisto-manifests/src/python.rs`, around lines 367-376.

Poetry allows dependency version specs like `^1.2`, `~1.2`, `*`, `1.*` in `pyproject.toml` (Poetry's own caret/tilde/wildcard syntax, a superset that isn't valid PEP 440). The current code tries to parse these directly as PEP 440 specs, which fails outright, and the dependency is silently dropped from the graph entirely — no warning, no error, the package just doesn't appear as a dependency. This is a real, high-severity bug: it means Callisto's version-bump cascade logic will not see (and therefore will not bump) packages that depend on a Poetry-style version constraint.

Read the surrounding code fully first — understand how PEP 440 specs are currently parsed and where the parse failure leads to the silent drop. Then implement a fix: normalize Poetry's caret (`^`), tilde (`~`), and wildcard (`*`, `1.*`) syntax into an equivalent PEP 440-compatible constraint (or a structurally equivalent internal representation) before/instead of the raw PEP 440 parse attempt, so these dependencies are correctly captured in the graph instead of silently disappearing. If a construct genuinely cannot be represented, it must fail loudly (a typed error), never silently disappear.

Reference semantics (standard Poetry caret/tilde rules):
- `^1.2.3` → `>=1.2.3, <2.0.0` (caret allows changes that don't modify the leftmost non-zero digit)
- `^0.2.3` → `>=0.2.3, <0.3.0` (leading zero majors: caret pins the leftmost non-zero digit, which may be minor or patch)
- `~1.2.3` → `>=1.2.3, <1.3.0` (tilde allows patch-level changes)
- `~1.2` → `>=1.2.0, <1.3.0`
- `*` → any version (equivalent to no constraint)
- `1.*` → `>=1.0.0, <2.0.0`

npm/pnpm workspace configs support glob negation (a leading `!` on a pattern excludes matching paths from an otherwise-included set, e.g. `workspaces: ["packages/*", "!packages/excluded-one"]`). You are fixing two confirmed, adversarially-verified bugs in the Callisto Rust monorepo (a release/versioning engine) related to release-group version computation. Work in your own git worktree (already checked out). Base your branch off `origin/main` (fetch first).

## Bug 1: `fixed_group_target` receives an unfiltered group, letting a stale member corrupt the alignment base

File: `crates/callisto-graph/src/cascade.rs`, around line 414.

Context: this codebase has both a "Linked" release-group mode and a "Fixed" release-group mode. The Linked-group code path already has a guard that filters out stale group members (packages tagged as part of the group but no longer live/current) before computing the group's version-alignment target — call this the "live_members" filter. The Fixed-group code path at line 414 does NOT apply the same filter: it passes the raw, unfiltered group `g` directly into `fixed_group_target`. If a group member is stale (still tagged with the group but no longer actually part of it, e.g. removed from the workspace or unlinked), its stale/leftover version data can silently corrupt the computed alignment base — the adversary agent that confirmed this traced a concrete scenario where the base gets computed as `1.0.0` instead of the correct aligned version, because the stale member's tag data pollutes the max/target computation.

Read `cascade.rs` fully first: find the Linked-group code path's stale-member guard (search for wherever `live_members` or an equivalent filter is applied before Linked-group target computation), and mirror the exact same filtering into the Fixed-group ("Track 1") code path at line 414, before the call to `fixed_group_target`. Do not just copy-paste blindly — read both code paths and confirm the filter predicate is semantically identical for both group kinds (a "live" member for a Fixed group should mean the same thing as for a Linked group — currently part of the workspace and not stale/orphaned).

Write a regression test that reproduces the corruption: construct a Fixed group with one live member and one stale/orphaned member, and assert the computed target version is the correct aligned version, NOT `1.0.0` (or whatever the corrupted fallback was). Also confirm the existing Linked-group tests still pass (no behavior change there).

## Bug 2: `ReleaseOperationId`'s `Ord` still compares `version.render()` (raw string) instead of proper `Version` equality

File: `crates/callisto-model/src/release.rs`.

Context: this codebase has a documented, previously-partially-fixed bug class where `Ord`/`Eq` consistency is violated for `BTreeSet`/`BTreeMap` keys — the invariant `a.cmp(b) == Equal` must imply `a == b` (and vice versa) was broken because a hand-written `Ord` impl compared some field via a lossy proxy (e.g. a rendered string) rather than the real semantic value. ## Bug 1: Lock-acquisition failure always blames "another release holds the lock"

File: `crates/callisto-vcs/src/release_lock.rs`, around line 52.

Read the surrounding code fully. Currently, ANY lock-acquisition failure (regardless of actual cause — e.g. permission denied, disk full, filesystem doesn't support the locking primitive used, I/O error, or an actually-held lock) is reported/asserted as specifically "another release holds the lock." This is misleading for every cause other than the true held-lock case. Find where the lock acquisition happens (likely a file-lock or similar OS-level primitive) and what error information is actually available at that point (check the underlying error type/kind — e.g. `std::io::ErrorKind`, or whatever lock library is used). Write tests proving: the specific "already locked" scenario still reports that this is due to another holder, AND a different failure cause (e.g. simulate a permission or generic I/O error) reports that different cause rather than the "another release holds the lock" message.

File: `crates/callisto-graph/src/identity.rs`, around lines 55-58 and 78-81.

File: `crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/add.rs`, line 34.

Current code: `CliError::Other(format!("Invalid severity \`{sev_str}\`. Must be patch, minor, or major."))`. ## Summary

**Commit:** `f531f624400a89ed8c9e9bd84791b7fe2dee435e`

### Bug 1 — `fixed_group_target` stale-member corruption
File: `crates/callisto-graph/src/groups.rs` (function signature) + `crates/callisto-graph/src/cascade.rs` (call site, line ~414).

Root cause confirmed by reading both group-kind code paths: the Fixed-group ("Track 1") block in `solve_cascade` already computed a filtered `live_members` list (for severity propagation), but then called `crate::groups::fixed_group_target(g, ...)` with the raw, unfiltered `GroupDef`. Inside `fixed_group_target`, `g.package_members()` picked `released[0]` from ALL declared members; if a stale member (absent from `input.base`) sorted first and still carried a leftover release tag, `base.get(&released[0])` missed and silently fell back to the hardcoded `Version::semver(1, 0, 0)`, corrupting the alignment target for every live sibling.

Fix: changed `fixed_group_target`'s first parameter from `g: &GroupDef` to `live_members: &[PackageId]`, so the call site passes the already-filtered list — mirroring the Linked-group block's existing guard and making the corruption structurally unrepresentable (no caller can pass an unfiltered group anymore). Investigation confirmed `render::attribution::attribution_line` (`crates/callisto-cli/src/render/attribution.rs`) had zero callers, while the spec (`docs/01-spec.md`, §13 invariant 28 / §CLI.5.2 / §CLI.5.3) explicitly mandates it be called from `render::<command>::human` "wherever a `BumpRecord`/`Diagnostic` carries a `governed_by`." `BumpRecord.governed_by` and `Diagnostic.governed_by` are real, populated fields in production (`callisto-graph/src/commands/version.rs`, `cascade.rs`, `aggregate.rs`), but `render_version` — the one function with real, non-`None` values to render — silently dropped them.

The fix was genuinely narrow: `render_version` and the shared `render_diagnostics` helper gained a `&ResolvedConfig`/`Option<&ResolvedConfig>` parameter respectively, with exactly one production call site (`commands/version.rs`) needing updates. All 5 other `render_diagnostics` callers (status/publish/publish_report/validate/matrix) pass `None` since none of those report kinds ever populate `governed_by` on a diagnostic today — documented as a deliberate, tracked deferral in the changeset rather than silently left out.

Added tests: 3 new unit tests for `attribution_line` itself (previously zero coverage), a wiring test in `render/mod.rs`, and an end-to-end test in `commands/version.rs` exercising the real `EmptyChangeset` diagnostic path. `cargo test -p callisto-cli` — 104 lib tests + all integration suites pass. `cargo clippy -p callisto-cli --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean. Changeset: `.changeset/wire-config-attribution-line-into-version-render.md` (minor).

**Finding 1 (`GraphError::ReleaseIntentStale` catch-all) — NOT FIXED, scoping report below. No code committed for this finding.**

This is systemic, not a handful of call sites. `ReleaseIntentStale` is constructed at **83 sites across 3 files** (`crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release.rs` ~60, `release_decision.rs` ~40, `release_execution.rs` 2), and it is nearly the *only* error variant these files use — `release.rs` alone has 39 `return Err(GraphError::...)` sites but only 6 distinct variants, one of which (`ReleaseIntentStale`) accounts for the overwhelming majority.

Confirmed miscategorization spans at least these distinct failure families, all currently collapsed onto one variant whose help text says "Regenerate and reapprove the release intent; no release operation was authorized":

- **Genuinely correct uses** (~8-10 sites): pre-dispatch re-observation of git trust/workspace state changing between reads (`recheck_trust`, `build_release_intent`, `validate_release_intent_with_state_directory`).
- **Post-dispatch mischaracterization** (the confirmed "provably false" case): `dispatch_registry`'s npm-publish-succeeded-but-registry-not-yet-consistent branch (release.rs:367) returns this error *after* a publish command already succeeded — the help text "no release operation was authorized" is false at that call site.

## Summary

Two confirmed, adversarially-verified bugs from the second-round audit shortlist, related to release-group version computation.

- **Fixed-group stale-member corruption**: `solve_cascade`'s Fixed-group ("Track 1") block passed the raw, unfiltered `GroupDef` into `fixed_group_target`, unlike the Linked-group block which already filters to live members. A group member removed from the workspace but still declared in `callisto.toml` — if it carried a leftover release tag — could be picked as the alignment base and silently fall back to `1.0.0` when its (missing) base-version lookup failed, corrupting the target for every live sibling. `fixed_group_target` now takes an already-filtered `live_members: &[PackageId]` slice, making the corruption structurally unrepresentable at the call site rather than just patched there.
- **`ReleaseOperationId`/`ArtifactSlotId` `Ord`/`Eq` inconsistency**: both hand-written `Ord` impls keyed their `Version` field on `.render()` alone, dropping `grammar`. The same literal string parses under more than one grammar (`"1.2.3"` is valid both as SemVer and PEP 440), so two `Eq`-distinct values could compare `Ordering::Equal`, violating the `BTreeSet`/`BTreeMap` invariant `a.cmp(b) == Equal` iff `a == b`. This is a residual instance of the same defect class fixed once before for `attestation_policy` (PR #64). Both now key on `(grammar, raw)` via a shared `version_ord_key` helper. `ArtifactSlotId` was a previously-unnoticed sibling of the same defect, found during this fix and corrected in the same commit.

## Test plan
- [x] `cargo nextest run -p callisto-graph -p callisto-model` — 710 passed, 0 skipped

- [x] New regression tests: stale-tagged-member-first scenario resolves to the correct aligned version (not `1.0.0`); grammar-distinct/render-identical `Version`s stay `Eq`-distinct under `Ord` for both types

content.text:
Main's post-merge CI just finished green too. Here's the full picture.

**Yes — `main` is releasable right now.** Everything's green:

- Main CI (post-#74 merge): all jobs pass, including the changeset/workspace validation.
- The release workflow already regenerated release PR **#55** (`callisto/version-packages`) to include #74's changeset — no manual step needed there, that's the forge-commit-API automation working as designed.
- The release preview targets a **0.7.0 minor bump** across all 10 packages, all backward-compatible, driven by the accumulated changesets from this session's audit-fix work plus earlier refactors.
- PRs #75, #76, #77 (Poetry/glob, error-accuracy, ConfigProvenance) all pass full CI independently and are conflict-free against current main (`mergeable: MERGEABLE`) — they're just waiting on your merge decision, not blocked by anything real.

**Will it work fine for "the next release"?** Two different meanings worth separating:

1. **If you cut a release right now** (merge #55): you get everything currently on `main` — all of PR #73/#74's fixes, but *not* #75/#76/#77 since those aren't merged yet. That's a perfectly safe release; it just won't include the Poetry/glob-negation fix or the error-message fixes yet.
2. **If you want those three included first**: merge #75/#76/#77 (any order, no conflicts), let the release workflow regenerate #55 again (automatic on each main push), then cut.

Nothing outstanding blocks a release either way — the only known unresolved issue (`ReleaseIntentStale` catch-all) is a diagnostic/error-message quality problem, not a correctness bug that would corrupt a release.

1	//! End-to-end coverage for the ConfigProvenance rendering fix: before it,
2	//! `render_version`'s text output never consulted `BumpRecord.governed_by`,
3	//! so an operator running the real CLI had no way to see which
4	//! `callisto.toml` key (or default) drove a cascade bump. The in-process
5	//! unit test next to the fix (`render/mod.rs`) proves `render_version`
6	//! itself is wired correctly against a hand-built `VersionReport`; this
7	//! test proves the attribution line survives all the way from a real
8	//! dependency graph, through the cascade solver, to the actual text a user
9	//! sees on stdout.
10	
11	use std::path::Path;
12	use std::process::Command;
13	
14	fn callisto_bin() -> &'static str {
15	    env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_callisto")
16	}
17	
18	fn git_init(root: &Path) {
19	    for args in [
20	        vec!["init", "-q", "-b", "main"],
21	        vec!["config", "user.name", "Callisto Tester"],
22	        vec!["config", "user.email", "tester@callisto.dev"],
23	        vec!["config", "commit.gpgsign", "false"],
24	        vec!["config", "tag.gpgsign", "false"],
25	    ] {
26	        assert!(Command::new("git")
27	            .args(&args)
28	            .current_dir(root)
29	            .status()
30	            .unwrap()
31	            .success());
32	    }
33	}
34	
35	fn git_commit_all(root: &Path, message: &str) {
36	    assert!(Command::new("git")
37	        .args(["add", "-A"])
38	        .current_dir(root)
39	        .status()
40	        .unwrap()
41	        .success());
42	    assert!(Command::new("git")
43	        .args(["commit", "-q", "-m", message])
44	        .current_dir(root)
45	        .status()
46	        .unwrap()
47	        .success());
48	}
49	
50	fn run_callisto_text(root: &Path, args: &[&str]) -> String {
51	    let output = Command::new(callisto_bin())
52	        .arg("--cwd")
53	        .arg(root)
54	        .args(args)
55	        .output()
56	        .expect("failed to spawn callisto binary");
57	    assert!(
58	        output.status.success(),
59	        "callisto {args:?} failed: {}",
60	        String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stderr)
61	    );
62	    String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout).into_owned()
63	}
64	
65	/// A cascade-driven bump (upstream-crate goes major, downstream-crate's
66	/// `"1.0"` requirement no longer covers it) must print a "governed by
67	/// [cascade].bump-severity" attribution line beneath the bump in the real
68	/// text renderer a user sees -- not just in a hand-constructed
69	/// `VersionReport` fed directly to `render_version` in a unit test.
70	#[test]
71	fn version_dry_run_text_output_shows_cascade_attribution_for_a_real_dependency_graph() {
72	    let dir = tempfile::tempdir().unwrap();
73	    let root = dir.path();
74	    git_init(root);
75	
76	    std::fs::write(
77	        root.join("Cargo.toml"),
78	        "[workspace]\nmembers = [\"crates/upstream-crate\", \"crates/downstream-crate\"]\nresolver = \"2\"\n",
79	    )
80	    .unwrap();
81	    std::fs::write(root.join("callisto.toml"), "").unwrap();
82	
83	    std::fs::create_dir_all(root.join("crates/upstream-crate/src")).unwrap();
84	    std::fs::write(
85	        root.join("crates/upstream-crate/Cargo.toml"),
86	        "[package]\nname = \"upstream-crate\"\nversion = \"1.0.0\"\nedition = \"2021\"\n",
87	    )
88	    .unwrap();
89	    std::fs::write(root.join("crates/upstream-crate/src/lib.rs"), "pub fn hello() {}\n").unwrap();
90	
91	    std::fs::create_dir_all(root.join("crates/downstream-crate/src")).unwrap();
92	    std::fs::write(
93	        root.join("crates/downstream-crate/Cargo.toml"),
94	        "[package]\nname = \"downstream-crate\"\nversion = \"1.0.0\"\nedition = \"2021\"\n\n[dependencies]\nupstream-crate = { path = \"../upstream-crate\", version = \"1.0\" }\n",
95	    )
96	    .unwrap();
97	    std::fs::write(root.join("crates/downstream-crate/src/lib.rs"), "pub fn world() {}\n").unwrap();
98	
99	    git_commit_all(root, "Initial commit");
100	
101	    let add_out = run_callisto_text(
102	        root,
103	        &[
104	            "add",
105	            "--package",
106	            "upstream-crate:major",
107	            "--summary",
108	            "breaking change",
109	        ],
110	    );
111	    assert!(add_out.contains("Added changeset"), "add did not succeed: {add_out}");
112	
113	    let plan_text = run_callisto_text(root, &["version", "--dry-run"]);
114	
115	    assert!(
116	        plan_text.contains("upstream-crate 1.0.0"),
117	        "upstream-crate's own bump must be listed: {plan_text}"
118	    );
119	    assert!(
120	        plan_text.contains("downstream-crate"),
121	        "downstream-crate must cascade since its \"1.0\" requirement no longer covers 2.0.0: {plan_text}"
122	    );
123	    assert!(
124	        plan_text.contains("governed by [cascade].bump-severity"),
125	        "the cascade-driven bump must print its ConfigProvenance attribution line in real CLI text output: {plan_text}"
126	    );
127	}

**Yes — this results in a working Callisto for your users, and I now have direct proof, not just passing tests.**

I built the real binary with all four fixes merged and ran it against realistic Poetry/npm/pnpm monorepo scenarios, then compared identical scenarios against the pre-fix binary:

- **Poetry cascade**: pre-fix binary silently leaves a dependent package at a stale version with a broken `^1.0` pin pointing at a version that no longer exists — no error, no warning. Fixed binary correctly cascades the bump with a governed-by attribution.
- **Glob negation**: pre-fix binary wrongly admits a package explicitly excluded via `!packages/excluded-one`. Fixed binary correctly excludes it.
- **Error messages**: confirmed old vs. new text directly.
- **GitHub Action**: both of its own contract-test suites (fake-boundary + real-binary-against-real-jq) pass in full against the combined fixed binary, and the production release workflow already ran successfully against #74's merge.

You were right that this needed checking — I also found a real gap you flagged: all four fixes had only unit/module-level tests, nothing exercising the actual CLI a user runs. I converted the exact scenarios I manually verified into permanent subprocess-level e2e tests (happy path, corner case, error case each), confirmed each one **fails against the pre-fix binary** (proving they're real regression tests, not vacuous), and pushed them onto PRs #75, #76, #77.

content.text:
# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.
